sentences.text: The name Lariosaurus means "Lizard from Larius," referring to the ancient name of Lake Como, and the animal was a primitive nothosaur characterized by a short neck and small flippers compared to its relatives.

A complete specimen of L. xingyiensis measured 70.5 cm long, while L. hongguoensis may have reached up to 80 cm, though some sources indicate that the size of Lariosaurus did not exceed 60 cm in length, making it one of the smallest known nothosaurs.

This creature had strongly elongated premaxillary and anterior dentary teeth resembling fangs that likely functioned as a fish trap, vertebrae that were pachyostotic and possessed low neural spines, and gastral ribs composed of multiple elements that formed a sturdy type of armor.
A Lariosaurus skeleton containing two juvenile Cyamodus placodonts in its stomach provides evidence of its diet.
Based on findings of immature skeletons inside adults, many believe Lariosaurus was viviparous and capable of bearing live young.
Lariosaurus was first discovered at Perledo on Lake Como in 1830 and named in 1847 by Curioni.
Due to its short neck and small flippers, Lariosaurus was likely a poor swimmer that spent much time on land or hunting in shallow waters.
Lariosaurus likely spent much of its life swimming in shallow waters or on the shore, catching small prey like fish, shrimp, crabs, and worms, or scavenging reptile eggs.
Lariosaurus lived during the Middle Triassic (late Anisian to late Ladinian stages) in central and western Europe and China.
While Rieppel synonymized Lariosaurus, Silvestrosaurus, and Ceresiosaurus in 1998, many authors dispute this and consider them close relatives instead.
